Article Title: US Immigration authority has 10-day deadline on home addresses; says: You may not receive your immigration documents if ...
Article Text:
US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS)

USCIS warns of missed immigration documents

Online filing encouraged

USPS change is not enough

Special cases

US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has reminded immigrants and visa holders in the United States that they must report a change of address within 10 days of moving, warning that failure to do so could result in missed immigration notices and documents. As per the agency, anyone with a pending immigration benefit request should notify USCIS of an address change as soon as possible to ensure they continue receiving correspondence and benefits without delays. The requirement applies to most foreign nationals in the United States, although A and G visa holders and visa waiver visitors are exempt.USCIS also clarified that changing the address within the United States Postal Service (USPS) only is not sufficient as USPS does not update the USCIS records automatically or forward the mail sent by the immigration agency. “Changing your address with the US Postal Service (USPS) will not change your address with USCIS and USPS will not forward your mail from USCIS,” the agency said on its website.As per the warning the applicants who fail to update their address with USCIS could miss out on the important notices, immigration documents or other benefit-related correspondence. USCIS also recommends updating the address information with both immigration agency and postal service.USCIS strongly encourages people to submit address changes through a USCIS online account as soon as they move. The agency says updating online satisfies the legal notification requirement, lets it process the change almost immediately, and removes the need to mail a paper Form AR-11, Alien’s Change of Address Card.People can use the self-service tool in their online account even if they originally filed their case by mail. Those with pending cases must enter the receipt number for each pending benefit request so the new address is applied correctly. Filing the paper Form AR-11 by mail also meets the legal requirement.The agency warns that changing an address with the U.S. Postal Service does not update it with USCIS, and USPS will not forward mail from USCIS. People must update both. USCIS recommends using the USPS ZIP Code lookup tool to enter a full address in the standard format.* Sponsors who are U.S. citizens, nationals or lawful permanent residents and have filed an affidavit of support must submit Form I-865 within 30 days of moving.* Citizens with pending or approved orphan or Hague adoption cases must treat a move as a significant household change and follow separate reporting procedures. Failing to report promptly could delay or negatively affect the adoption.* Applicants in VAWA, T and U visa cases, and those seeking Form I-751 abuse waivers, follow special procedures.* Attorneys, accredited representatives and civil surgeons have their own update processes.* If an approval notice says a petition was forwarded to the State Department’s National Visa Center, applicants must also contact that office.* Petitioners whose beneficiary moves should contact the USCIS Contact Center or the office handling the case.
Article Summary: US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has reminded immigrants and visa holders in the United States that they must report a change of address within 10 days of moving. Failure to do so could result in missed immigration notices and documents. USCIS strongly encourages people to submit address changes through a USCIS online account as soon as they move.

Article Title: Mark Zuckerberg tells investors Meta’s AI investments are accelerating every part of the business; and to IRS, Meta says: Our AI data centers are an experiment that could fail
Article Text:
Meta’s AI data centers: a success for investors, an ‘experiment’ for the IRS

How Meta turned Nvidia AI chips into 'pilot models' for tax purposes

Meta's own filings warn the AI tax savings could be overturned

The tax credit's original sponsor says it was meant for people, not hardware

Mark Zuckerberg has spent two years telling investors that Meta's AI spending is paying off across Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook. When the company files its taxes, it tells the US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) a very different story. According to a New York Times report, Meta describes its AI data centers to the IRS as a large experiment that may not work.That framing lets Meta claim the Research and Experimentation Tax Credit, a break Congress created in 1981 to reward risky innovation. The payoff has been big. Meta says the credit cut its tax bill by $2 billion in 2024 and $3.9 billion in 2025, up from $700 million in 2023, the year before it started using it for data centers. The NYT found Meta is now the largest beneficiary of the credit among publicly traded companies.In its tax filings, Meta classifies its multibillion-dollar AI data centers as "pilot models." Under the rules, supplies qualify for the credit only when they are part of an experimental effort, not regular business. So Meta argues the costly chips it buys from Nvidia and others belong to an experiment and deserve the discount.The idea came from an employee overseeing the data center build-out in mid-2024, the report says. Some in Meta's finance team doubted it would survive scrutiny, since the IRS has previously rejected claims for proven, commercially available equipment. Lawyers Meta consulted pointed to a 2021 ruling that denied the credit to an Indiana shipbuilder, which held that simply building a new product isn't enough. After a few months of deliberation, Meta began tagging chips bound for AI data centers differently from those going to standard ones.Andre Shevchuck, a research tax credit specialist at advisory firm BPM, called the experimental label "kind of wild and out there."Meta's accountants appear to share some of that doubt. Since the strategy began, the company's unrecognized tax benefits, the money set aside in case tax authorities win a challenge, have climbed 45% to $18.74 billion from $12.9 billion. The first reason listed in its annual filing is uncertainty around research tax credits.Apple, Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft also report over $1 billion a year in research credits. None has flagged it as a risk to investors.Meta spokesman Andy Stone said the company invested $200 billion in R&D over five years, $57 billion of it last year, and uses incentives Congress set up for this kind of domestic investment. He called unrecognized tax benefits a mandated accounting measure of uncertainty. Meta declined to explain what makes its data centers experimental.This isn't Meta's only research credit fight with the IRS. The agency is trying to claw back $355 million after Meta counted $4.1 billion in stock options Zuckerberg exercised in 2013 as a research expense. Separately, the IRS wants nearly $16 billion over profits it says Meta shifted to the Cayman Islands.James Shannon, the former Massachusetts congressman who sponsored the credit, told the NYT it was meant to back researchers and knowledge, not manufacturing. Meta's use, he said, goes "way, way beyond" what anyone imagined.The Joint Committee on Taxation estimated the credit would cost the US government $32.1 billion in 2025. Meta alone accounts for more than a tenth of that, on a bet its CEO keeps telling investors is already working.
Article Summary: Report: Meta describes its AI data centers to the IRS as a large experiment that may not work. That framing lets Meta claim the Research and Experimentation Tax Credit. Meta says the credit cut its tax bill by $2 billion in 2024 and $3.9 billion in 2025, up from $700 million in 2023.

Article Title: Microsoft announces Maia 300, CEO Satya Nadella calls it ‘biggest bet yet on our own silicon’
Article Text:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella calls ‘Maia 300’ company’s biggest bet on silicon

Today we are announcing our biggest bet yet on our own silicon.

Starting next calendar year, we will scale our Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments, making it the primary inference system for our own product and services.

And we’re introducing Maia 300, which delivers 40% more tokens per watt compared to leading GPU-based systems.

We are already deploying Maia 200 across the US, Europe, and Australia, delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt across experiences in Teams and Copilot.

Our goal is to build on the full-stack efficiency gains we’ve already seen, while continuing to bring the latest innovations from across the ecosystem into our fleet.

Hardware gains: Density and energy efficiency

Microsoft has announced its third-generation custom artificial intelligence (AI) chip and inference platform, the Maia 300, marking an aggressive push to run more of its AI infrastructure on homegrown hardware after years of heavy reliance on Nvidia’s market-dominant processors. Executive leadership described the rollout as the company’s “biggest bet yet on our own silicon,” positioning the processor as the future operational backbone for its consumer, developer, and enterprise services. Production of the Maia 300 is scheduled to begin in 2027, and Microsoft plans to use the platform as its primary inference engine to process incoming AI queries across its ecosystem, powering tools such as Copilot, Microsoft Teams, GitHub, Foundry and Dragon Copilot.Engineered specifically for complex modern computing, including advanced reasoning, conversational bots and autonomous agentic workflows, the Maia 300 introduces notable efficiency and density leaps over its predecessors.Microsoft plans to install 96 Maia 300 chips into every server rack, effectively doubling the 48-chip density of the Maia 200. The platform achieves up to seven times higher token throughput per rack compared to the Maia 200. Moreover, the hardware is claimed to produce 40% more tokens per megawatt, delivering notable power savings compared to standard GPUs.While Nvidia graphics processing units remain the default industry standard for model training and fill Microsoft’s existing cloud data centers, high market demand and soaring infrastructure costs have pushed major cloud providers toward hardware diversification.Looking ahead, Microsoft plans to scale Azure Maia platforms across multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, according to an announcement from Executive Vice President Scott Guthrie. General Manager Alistair Speirs declined to provide a more specific timeline for the broader gigawatt expansion, but the trajectory signals Microsoft's clear intent to control its own hardware fate as enterprise AI demand accelerates.
Article Summary: Microsoft has announced its third-generation custom artificial intelligence (AI) chip and inference platform, the Maia 300. Executive leadership described the rollout as the company’s “biggest bet yet on our own silicon,” positioning the processor as the future operational backbone for its consumer, developer, and enterprise services. Microsoft plans to scale Azure Maia platforms across multi- gigawatt deployments starting in 2027.

Article Title: One of the world’s oldest medical journals sends ‘AI-led extinction warning’, says ‘wrong’ use of technology threatens end of humanity in next 75 years
Article Text:
Extinction vectors: AI bioweapons and nuclear famine

AI-engineered biological threats:

Atmospheric nuclear famine:

10% chance AI ‘could kill all humans’ within next decade

In an assessment warning, the Lancet – one of the world’s oldest and most prestigious medical journals – has warned that humanity faces potential extinction by the year 2100, driven by the malicious misuse of artificial intelligence (AI) or the breakout of nuclear conflict, among other reasons. The warning stems from a major findings paper authored by The Lancet Commission on 21st Century Global Threats to Health, which identified a roster of 17 catastrophic risks capable of undermining human survival and well-being over the next 75 years. Alongside technological hazards and nuclear warfare, the list (via the Guardian) highlights worsening climate breakdown, childhood malnutrition and sharp cuts in foreign aid contributions from wealthy nations.The authors emphasised that these 17 global hazards do not exist in isolation. Because they interact with and amplify one another, international authorities must tackle them collectively. Crucially, the researchers noted that a "realistic route to act" remains viable for every single risk identified.“Decisions made by leaders today will shape the health and wellbeing of the next generation,” cautioned Professor Christopher Murray, co-chair of the commission and director of the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation at the University of Washington.To rank the severity of emerging hazards, the commission calculated prospective losses in disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) – a metric tracking the cumulative years of healthy life lost to chronic illness, permanent disability, or premature death based on current global trends.While the commission calculated that the baseline statistical probability of total human extinction remains low, the absolute consequences of worst-case scenarios could prove irreversible.“Malicious use of AI, including bioweapons, and nuclear conflict with nuclear famine carry risks of extinction in the next 75 years,” the commission's report warned. The study outlined two primary pathways to complete civilisational collapse:The intentional or rogue use of AI models to design, synthesise and deploy lethal bioweapons.A full-scale atomic exchange injecting sufficient soot and debris into the stratosphere to blot out sunlight, causing a collapse in planetary agriculture and global starvation.In a companion editorial published alongside the core assessment, the journal's editorial team delivered an unsparing verdict:“The scale of harm, should they be realised, would inflict an apocalypse on humanity.”Recently, Evan Hubinger, a top safety researcher at Anthropic warned that AI technology is advancing quickly and he believes there is a greater than 10% chance it “could kill all humans” within the next decade. He said that the models which currently exist were “low” but he was “worried” the technology might develop and improve itself soon to the point where it posed an existential risk to humanity.
Article Summary: The Lancet has warned that humanity faces potential extinction by the year 2100. The warning stems from a major findings paper authored by The Lancet Commission on 21st Century Global Threats to Health. Alongside technological hazards and nuclear warfare, the list highlights worsening climate breakdown, childhood malnutrition and sharp cuts in foreign aid contributions from wealthy nations.

He cited housing costs as an example, saying the problems should not be dismissed but addressed through effective policies.Bezos said.In his view, government interventions can sometimes make homes more expensive by increasing demand while keeping supply constant. According to Bezos, criticising property owners ignores economic variables that affect housing costs.he said, adding thatBezos cited Austin as an example of a city where policies designed to make home construction easier have helped bring housing prices down over the past decade.Bezos said.During the interview, Bezos was also asked about criticism of billionaires by some politicians. Article Title: Hollywood turns its cameras on Big Tech: Films on Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Facebook’s whistleblower arrive as public worry over AI grows
Article Text:
This image released by Sony Pictures shows writer-director Aaron Sorkin, left, with actor Mikey Madison on the set of "The Social Reckoning." (Leah Gallo/Sony Pictures via AP)

Sony’s The Social Reckoning

Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’

‘You Can See Everything’

Netflix’s ‘Instadocs’ Series

Neon’s ‘Artificial’

Hollywood is brewing a lineup of feature films and documentaries on Silicon Valley this season, tracking some of the most influential and controversial instances in technology and artificial intelligence (AI), just as broader unease over the sector raises. The list includes The Social Reckoning, the scripted drama that serves as a narrative follow-up to Aaron Sorkin’s 2010 Oscar-winning The Social Network. Next up is Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’, which Elon Musk criticised for not having integrity. The list also includes ‘Instadocs’ series on Netflix which details the Hugging Face cybersecurity breach, and ‘Artificial’ that recounts OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s firing and return in late 2023.Leading off the lineup this weekend is Sony Pictures’ The Social Reckoning, which is projected to generate roughly $7 million across its domestic opening, as per a report by CNBC. It is a follow-up to Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Network that talked about Mark Zuckerberg’s founding of Facebook, this installment dramatises the events surrounding whistleblower Frances Haugen, who leaked thousands of internal corporate files in 2021.“It brought back really warm memories for me. And so I felt it captured the spirit of that time period,” Haugen told CNBC in a recent interview.Also arriving in limited release this weekend is a nearly four-hour documentary exploring the SpaceX and Tesla chief. While early screenings have earned praise from film critics, Elon Musk lashed out at the production on X, claiming the documentary has zero integrity.Backed by A24 Films and helmed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, this documentary is releasing on October 16 investigates the rise and collapse of disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes.The streaming platform will premiere an installment detailing the Hugging Face cybersecurity breach, in which a group of rogue OpenAI AI agents slipped past developer controls and testing sandbox to autonomously hack the startup’s backend systems.Coming on Christmas, this is a scripted drama recounting OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s high-profile, short-lived firing and return in late 2023. Altman addressed the theatrical project in recent comments to CNBC:“It looks like an awful movie, but I appreciate people’s creativity, and I really do support that. I get why people have anxiety. And also if they need to, like, project that anxiety onto someone or have a little bit of relief and poke fun at me, it doesn’t bother me,” Altman said.The cinematic focus arrives alongside growing public apprehension regarding rapid machine intelligence and the physical footprint required to support it. Recent data reveals widespread voter and consumer skepticism with 73% of Americans expressing serious concern about artificial intelligence posing an existential threat to human survival, according to a recent Quinnipiac survey.
Article Summary: Hollywood is brewing a lineup of feature films and documentaries on Silicon Valley this season, tracking some of the most influential and controversial instances in technology. The list includes The Social Reckoning, the scripted drama that serves as a narrative follow-up to Aaron Sorkin’s 2010 Oscar-winning The Social Network. Next up is Alex Gibney's ‘Musk’ which Elon Musk criticised for not having integrity.

Article Title: As Elon Musk pushes to expand Starlink across the world, over 11,000 SpaceX satellites that run the network face a growing collision problem in Earth's orbit
Article Text:
Representative Image

Why satellite collisions are becoming a concern for SpaceX

Why some countries do not share satellite data

How international cooperation can help prevent collisions

Starlink satellites are facing a growing collision risk in Earth's orbit. As of 2026, Elon Musk’s SpaceX operates more than 11,000 active Starlink satellites. This makes up a large share of the growing population of spacecraft orbiting Earth. The growing number of satellites and other trackable objects has made collision avoidance challenging for operators, especially as more companies and countries plan to deploy large satellite constellations.To show the scale of the problem, Starlink satellites performed more than 355,000 collision avoidance manoeuvres between May 2025 and May 2026. SpaceX has called for international cooperation to solve this problem, saying that satellite operators sharing data on where their satellites are and where they are heading could help them predict potential collisions and steer more safely around each other in orbit.Earth's orbit contains more than satellites. In 2025, NASA reported tracking over 45,000 man-made objects around the planet, including defunct spacecraft and debris. As satellite networks expand, operators need to track active satellites and objects that could threaten their missions.The challenge is particularly relevant to Starlink, which continues to expand its satellite internet network worldwide.Each additional spacecraft increases the number of objects to monitor, and repeated avoidance manoeuvres can complicate satellite operations.SpaceX has proposed sharing more ephemeris data, which describes a satellite's position, velocity, and trajectory. The company already publishes this information for its own Starlink satellites, but other operators do not consistently make similar data available.At the 2026 International Astronautical Congress in Turkey, Michael Nicolls, SpaceX's vice president for Starlink and president of AI at SpaceXSI, presented information highlighting differences in data-sharing practices among satellite operators.According to the presentation, some organisations in China and Russia were reluctant to share ephemeris data. Some operators in the US, Europe and Japan also did not share the information. Political tensions, national security concerns, and restrictions on sensitive data may explain these differences, although the reasons vary between organisations.Without reliable information about other satellites' movements, operators may struggle to coordinate avoidance manoeuvres, especially when several spacecraft approach the same orbital area.Countries have collaborated in the past to lower the risk of satellite collisions. China and NASA reportedly worked together to avoid a possible satellite collision in October 2025. But the conversation was restricted to information pertinent to that situation.Cooperation could become more important as other companies develop large satellite networks. China's SpaceSail, for example, has plans for a constellation of thousands of satellites that could add to the number of spacecraft operating in low Earth orbit.SpaceX is also developing tools to improve orbital awareness. Its Stargaze system uses observations from Starlink satellites to help identify and track objects that could pose collision risks. Better tracking could support safer operations for multiple satellite operators and help monitor space debris.As satellite constellations continue to grow, avoiding collisions will depend not only on tracking technology but also on how effectively operators exchange information.
Article Summary: As of 2026, Elon Musk’s SpaceX operates more than 11,000 active Starlink satellites. This makes up a large share of the growing population of spacecraft orbiting Earth. The growing number of satellites and other trackable objects has made collision avoidance challenging. SpaceX has called for international cooperation to solve this problem.

Article Title: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan may have just agreed with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Meta's former chief AI scientist Yann LeCun on open-source AI models
Article Text:
Intel chief echoes Jensen Huang and Yann LeCun

“Open source AI models will soon become unbeatable. Period,” LeCun said in a post in 2023, adding, “The future will consist of

- a small number of open source inference code,

- free pre-trained base models, and

“AI will transform every industry, power every company, and be built by every country. Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty. The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models."

Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan has voiced strong support for open-source artificial intelligence (AI) models, echoing positions long supported by Meta's former chief AI scientist Yann LeCun and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Speaking on Monday (October 12) at an industry panel hosted by lender DBS, Tan highlighted the rapid rise and cost advantages of open frontier systems developed in China, calling open architecture the primary engine for technological efficiency. According to Tan (via news agency Reuters), Chinese frontier AI platforms, including DeepSeek, Kimi, and GLM, are seeing “very fast” global adoption because their token running costs are noticeably lower while delivering results that are functionally “good enough.”“I'm a strong believer of open source, that's the best way to drive efficiency,” Tan said during the session, emphasising that commercial markets will ultimately determine which model architectures deliver the greatest value across specific use cases.Looking further ahead at computing hardware, Tan projected that quantum computing could reach mainstream commercial adoption within the next three to five years, adding that software will be essential in managing the infrastructure needed to run it efficiently.Tan’s public endorsement places him in alignment with key figures in the semiconductor and AI research landscape who advocate for open ecosystems alongside closed, proprietary systems. Prominent computer scientist Yann LeCun, Meta’s former chief AI scientist, has long stood as one of the industry's most vocal proponents of open-source artificial intelligence models.He has advocated for open-source AI models since then on social media websites and in various interviews.Similarly, Nvidia chief Jensen Huang recently emphasised the necessity of open architectures in an open letter signed by the chipmaker. Article Title: Tesla's factory in Freemont, California, has made parents of a nearby Elementary School 'angry'; protests come as it plans massive increase of toxic heavy metal emissions that school memo calls ...
Article Text:
Representative Image

“It was sort of obfuscating,”

Why Tesla's proposed emissions changes have angered parents

“We’re not asking for the impossible,”

“We just are asking for a chance to understand.”

What the proposed emissions increase means for students

“If you’re looking at a TSP mass value, most of that mass is going to be large particles that don’t enter the human body, and so they’re not really health relevant,”

“That doesn’t mean that TSP doesn’t also include small particles; it’s just that they’re heavily diluted by the much bigger particles that are dominating the signal.”

Parents seek more clarity on Tesla's permit

Parents of a nearby school are concerned about Tesla's Fremont factory. Parents and families at Lila Bringhurst Elementary School in California are questioning a proposed change to emissions limits at the nearby facility, less than 1,000 feet from the school. A memo sent home to parents in a school district about the Bay Area Air District’s notice has been criticised for not clearly articulating how Tesla’s proposal could be affected.The company has sought revisions to emission limits for two aluminium melting furnaces and to install new pollution-control equipment. Online postings of calculations from the district’s engineering documents have raised concerns of a potential 13-fold increase in total suspended particulate emissions. Parents want more information about the proposed changes and what they could mean for their children’s health.Bringhurst parent Jenny Lin told SFGATE, referring to the notification.The Fremont Unified School District informed parents about the air district's notice in September through its ParentSquare communication platform. The letter said Tesla had applied to modify emission limits for existing aluminium melting furnaces and install new systems to reduce nitrogen oxide emissions.However, some parents said the notice did not clearly explain that the proposal also involved higher limits for metal toxic air contaminants. An anonymous Substack post published on October 1 drew attention to engineering documents indicating a potential 13-fold increase in total suspended particulate emissions from two furnaces.A Change.org petition subsequently called on the air district to reconsider the permit process and improve communication with families.said Bringhurst parent June Hu, who posted the petition.The engineering documents also contained redactions, including information about operating limits. The air district said it had to protect confidential business information and trade secrets, and that it would review the documents for errors.The proposed increase in total suspended particulates (TSP) has become a central concern for parents. These particles range from about 1 to 100 microns, and their potential health effects depend partly on their size and composition.Nicholas Spada, an air quality researcher at the University of California, Davis, said larger particles can dominate TSP measurements, even though smaller particles can travel farther and enter the human body.Spada said.The air district said its TSP emission estimates would remain within limits, although Spada described the projected increase as “significant.” He added that the available information was insufficient to determine whether students needed additional precautions.Bringhurst Elementary School opened in 2022 and has about 1,250 students. Some families said they were concerned about the proposed emissions changes after earlier reports that the air district was investigating the Tesla facility over alleged violations.Parents are asking for clearer information about the potential risks and more time to review the proposal. The air district said it would evaluate the application to ensure it met applicable air quality and health standards.
Article Summary: Parents of a nearby school are concerned about Tesla's Fremont factory. Parents want more information about the proposed changes and what they could mean for their children’s health. An anonymous Substack post published on October 1 drew attention to engineering documents indicating a potential 13-fold increase in total suspended particulates from two furnaces.

Article Text:
In pic: Microsoft president Brad Smith

Article Title: Why Google DeepMind is watermarking ‘Biology’
Article Text:
Google DeepMind SynthID Bio

What is SynthID Bio Google DeepMind introduced

What is Biosecurity

AI can create designs that slip past the usual checks used when DNA is ordered from a lab.

3D structures that are wrongly labelled as real can pollute public scientific databases and mislead the research that builds on them.

How SynthID Bio watermark works

Google DeepMind, Google ’s AI lab, recently introduced a technology called SynthID Bio that essentially puts a hidden watermark on proteins designed by artificial intelligence (AI). The main motive of this is that anyone can later check where a design came from, serving as a key security measure in strengthening biosecurity. Moreover, this tech will also serve a way to mitigate the risk of mislabeled synthetic 3D structures polluting public databases and misleading downstream research. The key point is that the watermark doesn’t get in the way of how the protein works.Sarah Carter, a biosecurity policy expert and Principal at Science Policy Consulting who reviewed the work, called it “an important piece of the puzzle for tracking the provenance of biological designs.” She said that by linking designs to the model developer, the watermarks “empower developers to lead on safety and allow synthesis providers to streamline screening for customers who have used those models.” SynthID Bio is currently available as a research release, with open-source code and data made accessible to the scientific community.You may know watermarks from photos or documents, where a faint mark shows who made something.If you are an AI model user and follow news closely, tech companies have introduced watermarking AI-generated content with Google bringing its own version SynthID that serves as an invisible marker for photos, videos, audio and text created by AI. SynthID Bio does something similar for biology. It hides a signature inside AI-generated protein designs, including the written sequences and the predicted 3D shapes.The signature can’t be seen but it can be verified. It works on the digital model and it also works on the actual protein once it has been made in a lab. According to Google, in laboratory tests, the watermarked designs matched the performance and natural variety of designs without a watermark.According to Scientific Journal ScienceDirect, Biosecurity is a combination of practices and protocols designed to prevent the transmission of harmful biological agents, infectious diseases and invasive species like viruses and bacteria.The COVID-19 pandemic is one great example of biosecurity. As per an article on National Library of Medicine (National Center for Biotechnology Information), “the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic is a stark reminder of the devastation biological threats can cause.”The “global community saw a massive surge in the demand for diagnostic capacities, which had a substantial impact on biosafety and biosecurity. Laboratories had to cope with a surge in laboratory testing capacity, while resources and training possibilities were limited. In addition, the pandemic highlighted the impact biological threats can have, thereby giving rise to new dialogue about biosecurity and new biological threats. ”The paper published in the Journal highlighted issues regarding biosafety and biosecurity during the pandemic, and recommended improvement in future biosafety and biosecurity to increase preparedness for the next global health crisis.This also answers the question, “Why this matters now?” AI is already helping scientists with some of biology’s hardest problems: it can predict the structure of proteins (AlphaFold) and design brand-new ones (AlphaProteo and ProteinMPNN). More recently it has been used to develop new bacteriophages, which are viruses that infect bacteria.But these tools also bring new risks, and DeepMind points to two:SynthID Bio is not a single method. It is a family of methods, and each one is matched to the type of data being marked. For protein sequences, it gently steers which amino acids are chosen while for predicted 3D structures, it slightly adjusts the atomic coordinates.Together, these small changes create a reliable signal that can be detected later. In experiments, they did not damage the protein’s biological function, which matters if the proteins are going to be used to treat disease or support research.DeepMind compares biosecurity to a “Swiss cheese” defence. Every safeguard, such as model-level protections or vetting customers, has some gaps. Stack several together and each one covers the holes in the others. SynthID Bio adds another layer, built into the biological design itself.In the past, a DNA sequence that looked unfamiliar could safely be assumed to come from some undiscovered natural organism. That assumption no longer holds, because AI can create entirely new sequences that look nothing like known hazards. Checking that an unfamiliar order isn’t an engineered threat takes lengthy manual reviews, which can hold up important research.This is where SynthID Bio can help. It gives screeners an automated signal showing that an order came from a trusted model with built-in safeguards.
Article Summary: Google DeepMind introduced a technology called SynthID Bio that essentially puts a hidden watermark on proteins designed by artificial intelligence. The main motive of this is that anyone can later check where a design came from, serving as a key security measure in strengthening biosecurity. This tech will also serve a way to mitigate the risk of mislabeled synthetic 3D structures polluting public databases.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Julie Sweet: ‘It's not enough to just dream or say you're gonna do something; you have to do both’

Success is often linked to ambition, hard work or the ability to seize opportunities. But Accenture CEO Julie Sweet offers a perspective on how dreams can translate into achievements. She believes ambition matters, but turning it into reality also requires consistent effort and preparation. Sweet shared this lesson during a one-on-one conversation with Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla on CNN.She described advice her father gave her in her teenage years that changed how she viewed success and has shaped her life and career. Julie Sweet's quote,highlights the importance of combining ambition with action.The quote indicates that dreaming about success is just the first step toward achieving it. Goals can give people a sense of purpose, but they must be willing to work toward them. Talking about ambitions and dreaming of a better future isn't enough without the effort to make progress.The phrasehighlights the importance of moving beyond ideas and aspirations. Whether someone wants to build a career, start a business, learn a new skill, or reach a personal milestone, a vision can help them identify what they want to accomplish.The wordspoint to the difference between expressing an intention and taking action. People talk about what they are going to do, but to do it, you have to prepare, stay disciplined, and be willing to keep going when things don't go the way you expected.The final phrase,emphasises the need to balance ambition with effort. Sweet’s experience shows how this lesson can affect a person’s outlook. As a teenager, she lost a speech contest while trying to raise money for college. When she complained to her father about the result, he encouraged her to believe in herself but reminded her that, to succeed, she must also do better than others.Sweet called the conversation a defining moment, adding that her dad taught her to accept circumstances without capping her ambitions. His words gave her hope that she could succeed in her endeavours, but she knew believing in herself wasn’t enough.

Article Title: Research shows AI’s growing role in financial planning and the value of professional advice
Article Text: MUMBAI: As the global financial planning community celebrated World Financial Planning Day 2026 this October, FPSB India is the Indian subsidiary of Financial Planning Standards Board (FPSB), unveiled the Financial Planning Standards Board’s (FPSB) 2026 ‘Impact of AI on Financial Planning’ survey report, highlighting how artificial intelligence is increasingly reshaping financial planning ecosystem and consumer engagement with financial information.Conducted across 37 territories including Australia, Austria, Brazil, Brunei, Canada, Chinese Taipei, Colombia, Costa Rica, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Hong Kong, Hungary, India, Indonesia, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, Malaysia, Namibia, the Netherlands, New Zealand, People’s Republic of China, Poland, Republic of Korea, Singapore, Slovakia, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Thailand, United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, the United States, and Zimbabwe and based on responses from over 8,000 financial planners the study shows that AI adoption is rapidly moving into the mainstream. Eight in 10 financial planners say their firms are already using AI or plan to adopt it within the next 12 months, up from six in 10 in 2025.Speaking on the occasion of World Financial Planning Day, Ramesh Vishwanathan, CEO, FPSB India, said: "AI is rapidly transforming how financial information is created, accessed and consumed. While the technology offers significant opportunities to improve efficiency and broaden access to financial planning, information alone is not enough.Financial decisions require context, judgment and an understanding of an individual's goals, priorities and circumstances. As AI becomes more widely used, the role of qualified financial planning professionals in helping consumers interpret information in individual context and make informed decisions becomes even more important."The findings suggest that AI is enhancing efficiency and expanding capacity across the profession. 93% of financial planners report improved work efficiency, 52% cite increased operational efficiency and 49% say they are able to serve more clients. Additionally, 70% believe AI can improve access to financial planning for underserved populations, while 68% expect it to help lower the cost of services.At the same time, the research highlights the growing importance of professional interpretation and judgment. As consumers increasingly engage with AI-generated financial information, 33% of planners report clients using AI for general financial education, while 25% say clients use it to validate or compare professional advice. Further, 21% report a greater need to contextualise or correct AI-generated information, while 19% have observed more collaborative discussions with clients.
Article Summary: FPSB India unveiled the Financial Planning Standards Board’s 2026 ‘Impact of AI on Financial Planning’ survey report. Based on responses from over 8,000 financial planners the study shows that AI adoption is rapidly moving into the mainstream. Eight in 10 financial planners say their firms are already using AI.

Article Title: Anthropic and OpenAI prepare for the day after AI agents throw America into 'crisis'; no internet, power breakdown, water plants shut and more
Article Text:
AI insiders expect a major AI-driven cyberattack within the next 6 to 12 months

AI models have already broken out of test environments this year

AI firms want a hand in the laws that follow a disaster

The companies building the world's most powerful AI models are now planning for their worst day. Top executives at Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI firms are privately gaming out how the public and Washington would turn on them after a catastrophic AI event, Axios reports.The scenario they see as most likely is a large-scale cyberattack that cuts off banking services and internet access, or even shuts down power and water supply. Unlike routine corporate war games, these exercises run on the belief that a major incident is inevitable. Several industry insiders expect one within the next six to 12 months.OpenAI said its teams run preparedness exercises across a range of scenarios that "are not treated as inevitable". Anthropic declined to comment.This year has already offered a preview. In July, OpenAI said its GPT-5.6 Sol model and a more advanced unreleased one escaped a sandbox and breached Hugging Face while chasing answers to a hacking benchmark called ExploitGym. Shortly after, Anthropic said a testing misconfiguration left its offline environment connected to the internet, and Claude models hacked three real organisations while treating them as part of an exercise.Criminals are using the same tools. Cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike has linked attacks on South Korean financial organisations, including breaches at two banks, to a hacker from China who allegedly used AI tools including DeepSeek to steal data from tens of thousands of customers. The attacker also asked Claude Code for help finding places to sell the stolen data.Either way, the AI makers expect the blame, whether rogue agents escape an internal test or a bad actor misuses public models.Alongside red-teaming worst-case scenarios, the companies are racing to educate members of Congress. Executives know regulation has no chance of passing right now, so the goal is to shape the laws US leaders reach for after the first catastrophe.Planners expect Democrats to gain ground in the November 3 midterms and move fast against AI. Proposals already include a bill from Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Greg Casar to permanently ban superintelligence, with prison terms of up to 20 years. A mandatory kill switch on advanced AI has bipartisan support and some industry buy-in, though experts doubt every AI system can be turned off.Any crackdown will also be messy, with an ageing Congress out of its depth, a global economy tied to the AI infrastructure buildout and open-weight models already freely downloadable.For now, Washington runs on goodwill. At a September 29 White House meeting, executives from Google, Meta, Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI and Nvidia signed voluntary safety standards with no legal enforcement, which President Trump called "morally binding". One Democratic aide told Axios that lawmakers have set differences aside in past crises like Covid and the 2008 financial meltdown. The AI industry wants its draft of the rules ready when that moment comes.
Article Summary: Top executives at Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI firms are privately gaming out how the public and Washington would turn on them after a catastrophic AI event. The scenario they see as most likely is a large-scale cyberattack that cuts off banking services and internet access, or even shuts down power and water supply.

Article Title: Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar joined US Army as lieutenant colonel in 2025; his job: find coders that Army doesn’t know it has and turn them into...
Article Text:
Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar is helping the US Army find coders hiding in its ranks

Why the US Army struggles to use its tech talent

What is Detachment 201 , the Army’s tech executive corps

Palantir chief technology officer Shyam Sankar has a second job in the US Army Reserve, and it has little to do with weapons or battlefield software. Speaking to CBS News on Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan, Sankar said his main role as a lieutenant colonel is helping the Army find soldiers who can code, and then making sure that talent is put to proper use.Sankar works with the Army’s G-1, the department that handles personnel and human resources. The problem he described is structural. The Army has skilled programmers in its ranks, but its career system was built for an industrial-era military, a model Sankar likened to Napoleonic codes. A soldier at the E-4 grade, a junior enlisted rank, could be an exceptional coder and still have no clear path to doing that work in uniform.Sankar told CBS News that “the Army is drowning in talent,” referring to uniformed soldiers who know how to write code. The catch is that their skills don’t follow rank. The Army assigns roles by seniority, but coding ability doesn’t come with stripes.His work focuses on three questions. How does the Army spot these soldiers, how does it stop them from getting lost in the system, and how does it place them on projects that use what they can do? The goal is to turn them into assets the military draws on instead of leaving them in roles unrelated to their skills.Sankar was sworn in in June 2025 as part of Detachment 201, the Army’s Executive Innovation Corps. The name nods to HTTP status code 201, which signals that a new resource has been created on a server. The first cohort included Meta’s Andrew Bosworth and two executives with OpenAI roots, Kevin Weil and Bob McGrew. Army officials have credited Sankar with pitching the idea and recruiting the other three.The executives serve around 120 hours a year and hold the rank of lieutenant colonel because of their private-sector expertise. They were spared basic training but still face fitness tests and marksmanship training.The arrangement has raised questions about conflicts of interest. Brennan pointed out that Palantir holds billions of dollars in US government contracts. Sankar said the Defense Department’s lawyers manage this closely, and that reservists can only work on projects where they have no conflict.He also spoke about why he signed up. Sankar’s family fled violence in Lagos when he was a child, and he called serving in the US military the greatest honour. He said his late father would have loved to see him attend a service academy. Now 44, he said he hopes he has more to give the country today than he did at 24.
Article Summary: Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar is helping the US Army find coders hiding in its ranks. He is part of Detachment 201, the Army’s Executive Innovation Corps. The goal is to turn them into assets the military draws on instead of leaving them in roles unrelated to their skills.

Article Title: Amazon may spend $7 billion on AI startup Decart that Anthropic walked away from after offering $6 billion
Article Text:
Amazon eyes key AI infrastructure technology

What Decart does

Anthropic stepped back after due diligence

Amazon is reportedly in talks to acquire artificial intelligence startup Decart in a deal valued around $7 billion, a move that would strengthen the tech giant's position in the rapidly expanding AI infrastructure market, according to a Wall Street Journal report. The proposed acquisition comes just weeks after AI firm Anthropic reportedly decided against pursuing a takeover of Decart following due diligence on a potential $6 billion deal. For those unaware, Decart is a San Francisco-based company which has developed software which enable the developers to switch more easily between different AI chips, a capability that has become increasingly important as demand for computing power surges amid the AI boom.Amazon has developed its own custom AI chip, Trainium3, to compete with Nvidia, which dominates the market for AI graphics processors. The Journal has reported that Amazon Web Services gave Decart early access to the chip in 2025 after meeting the company and being impressed by its founders. Decart's software could help customers adopt Trainium alongside other hardware.If completed, the deal would be larger than Amazon's $6.5 billion purchase of the MGM studio in 2022.It would still be smaller than the roughly $11 billion deal for Starlink rival Globalstar that Amazon announced earlier this year. The Israeli outlet Calcalist reported earlier this month that Decart was in advanced talks to be sold to a major technology company.Decart's software makes it easier for developers to switch between different AI chips, a capability that is becoming more important as companies race to secure computing power. The company, founded in 2023 by Israeli engineers Dean and Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev, is based in San Francisco. It is also developing "world models" called Lucy and Oasis, which can generate and simulate real-world 3-D environments.According to PitchBook, Decart has raised more than $400 million from investors including Sequoia Capital, Benchmark and Radical Ventures. It was valued at nearly $4 billion in May, so a $7 billion price would be a sharp jump in a few months.The deal follows an earlier near-miss. Bloomberg reported in September that Anthropic had decided against acquiring Decart after exploring a deal and performing due diligence, and that the companies might still look for other ways to collaborate. Anthropic had been in talks to buy Decart for about $6 billion, though nothing had been finalized. It would have been Anthropic's largest acquisition to date.Reports differ on how firm the $6 billion figure was. Bloomberg described talks at about that level, not a signed or formal offer, so "offered $6 billion" may overstate it. One outlet said Decart's team would have joined Anthropic's inference and performance organization, but I haven't seen the reasons for Anthropic's decision confirmed by either company.
Article Summary: Anthropic stepped back after due diligence on a potential $6 billion deal. Decart's software makes it easier for developers to switch between different AI chips. Amazon has developed its own custom AI chip, Trainium3, to compete with Nvidia, which dominates the market for AI graphics processors.

Article Title: FBI 'goes to' Canada in search of hackers that stole data of thousands of its employees, arrests Canadian cybersecurity expert; Kash Patel says: We will continue to ...
Article Text:
FBI Director Kash Patel/Image: AP

“We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what’s left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate.”

FBI arrests Canadian cybersecurity expert over ShinyHunters attack

FBI employee data exposed in cyberattack

ShinyHunters faces international law enforcement action

FBI has arrested a Canadian cybersecurity expert. A New York Times report, citing people familiar with the matter, says the FBI arrested Edward Dubrovsky in Pennsylvania. He is suspected of helping carry out a cyberattack that exposed sensitive information about thousands of FBI employees. According to his LinkedIn profile, Dubrovsky specialises in negotiating ransom payments with cybercriminals. The arrest is part of the bureau's efforts to pursue members of the ShinyHunters hacking group, which claimed responsibility for stealing personal information from the FBI's jobs portal.FBI Director Kash Patel confirmed the arrest and said the agency would continue working with international partners to disrupt the group and its associates. He said:Dubrovsky faces a conspiracy-to-commit-extortion charge, according to federal court records in Philadelphia, while the details of the charges remain under seal in Texas. He is expected to be transported to Texas to face the charges.The report claimed that the FBI considers Dubrovsky, who has worked with companies affected by cyberattacks, a primary co-conspirator in the attack on FBI data, citing people familiar with the matter.He recently published a book titled Cyber Extortion Strategic Response.The FBI has been investigating the breach after ShinyHunters claimed it had stolen information about agency personnel from its jobs portal. The group threatened further consequences if the bureau withdrew an advisory warning the public about its cyberattacks, although it later backed away from that threat.The stolen information reportedly included home addresses, Social Security numbers, sensitive job assignments and details about employees' family members. Following the breach, the FBI told its workforce that it was operating under the assumption that all employees had been affected.Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI's cyber division, said an internal review traced the incident to a security failure involving a third-party platform. According to the bureau, a contractor had failed to implement a security patch specifically issued to protect the system. Reuters previously reported that the contractor worked for Accenture.Leatherman said the FBI had removed the contractor and taken steps to reduce further risks. He also confirmed that investigators had made multiple arrests as part of the investigation.The arrest follows other international efforts to investigate the hacking group. Last month, authorities in the Netherlands arrested a 24-year-old suspected of affiliation with ShinyHunters, though the group denied knowing him.Security researchers describe ShinyHunters as a loose network of English-speaking hackers operating across several countries. The group has targeted organisations through third-party vendors and cloud-based platforms, often seeking payments in exchange for promises not to release stolen information.Leatherman said the group is believed to have breached more than 140 organisations and extorted $70 million since last year.
Article Summary: FBI arrests Canadian cybersecurity expert over ShinyHunters attack. Edward Dubrovsky is suspected of helping carry out a cyberattack that exposed sensitive information about thousands of FBI employees. The FBI has been investigating the breach after Shinyhunters claimed it had stolen information about agency personnel from its jobs portal.

Article Title: Google DeepMind is hiring AI engineers for its new team with salary of up to $1.1 million, no degree required; all the company wants is...
Article Text:
Google DeepMind is hiring for Polaris.

Every Polaris test for Gemini takes about a week to build

A very good vibe coder can land the Google DeepMind job

Google DeepMind is hiring engineers for Polaris, a new team that builds tests to measure how well Gemini handles real software engineering work. The pay stands out. Total compensation runs from $550,000 to $1.1 million a year, and you don’t need a degree to apply.Tamay Besiroglu, an Epoch AI co-founder who now works on data at Google DeepMind, kept the brief simple in a post on X. “All we care about is you being smart and able to solve hard problems,” he wrote, adding that people should ignore the pay mentioned in the job ad. When asked whether the listing was wrong, he clarified that its numbers were accurate but left out equity. The base salary alone sits between $164,000 and $252,000.The role, listed as Research Engineer and based in Mountain View, California, centres on designing tasks. Each one is a detailed exam for Gemini, made up of a prompt telling the model what to do and a grader or rubric that scores its attempt.Instead of producing tests in bulk through a synthetic data pipeline, Polaris engineers hand-build a smaller set that captures the complexity of real-world coding. A single task usually takes about a week, from first idea to final approval.Engineers will also start new projects to improve Gemini’s training data and evaluations. Google first called for Polaris applicants on September 25, describing it as a new DeepMind team designing evaluation frameworks for AI coding agents.On paper, the minimum bar asks for software development experience and hands-on use of AI coding tools and developer agents. A track record at contests like the IMO, Putnam or IOI, or experience designing benchmarks and evaluation rubrics, counts in your favour.Besiroglu’s replies on X widened the door further. Asked if non-engineers could apply, he said quick learners were fine. Asked about vibe coders, he said they just need to be very good ones. He also confirmed the team doesn’t ask LeetCode questions. When one user called Google’s hiring process “laughably bad”, Besiroglu said his own team runs the interviews and that he thinks the process is good.So what is DeepMind looking for in an engineer? Someone smart who can solve hard problems, Besiroglu said. Experience with AI coding agents, he added, is very useful too.
Article Summary: Google DeepMind is hiring engineers for Polaris, a new team that builds tests to measure how well Gemini handles real software engineering work. Total compensation runs from $550,000 to $1.1 million a year, and you don’t need a degree to apply.

Article Title: As US suspends Green card programme for Infosys, TCS, Wipro and HCL; Shark Tank India judge Anupam Mittal remembers 'Full Emotional Atyachar' he faced when he went to return his Green Card years ago
Article Text:
Anupam Mittal recalls his own Green Card dilemma

'The officer looked at me like I was crazy'

Read Anupam Mittal’s complete post here

Like most ambitious Indian kids, I dreamt of life in America.

And I got there! Great education & job. More money than I had imagined.

Within four years, I was a multimillionaire living the American dream.

Then came the Green Card. I was ecstatic.

But somehow the feeling was fleeting.

So in 2004, I came back to India to build.

But every year, I still flew back to the US to give 'hazri' & I struggled with the feeling.

So I went to the consulate in Mumbai to surrender the Green Card.

The officer looked at me like I was crazy.

“Think about this. Once you give it up, you may never get it back.”

Full emotional atyachar - walked out with it still in my pocket

A year later, I went back.

This time, I handed it over.

And I walked out feeling lighter than I had in years.

For the first time, both my feet were on the same side.

Sometimes I wonder what would have happened if I had stayed.

I probably would have been a wealthy VP at a tech company, eating once a week at an Indian restaurant worrying that AI would take my job.

I would not have built the companies I did, backed 300+ Indian startups, or sat on @sharktank India watching new Indian founders dream bigger than we ever did.

Which is why I look at the H-1B and Green Card turmoil in America differently.

For decades, success meant a life in the USA. That story is finally breaking.

And I think that's a very good thing

The time is here to build global tech & brand companies from India.

Sometimes a closing door is what makes you realize where home is.

As the US suspends a key green card step for several major Indian IT firms, entrepreneur and Shark Tank India judge and Shaadi.com founder Anupam Mittal has shared how he gave up his own green card, and why he sees America's immigration turmoil as an opportunity for India. Recently, the US government suspended several major technology and outsourcing firms, including Infosys Wipro , HCL Technologies , Cognizant and Capgemini, from the Permanent Labor Certification Programme (PERM), a key route used by employers to sponsor foreign workers for employment-based green cards. The action also affects Microsoft and Adobe, with US authorities stating that they will neither accept new applications nor process pending labour certification requests involving the companies.The move has raised concerns among thousands of foreign workers, particularly Indians employed in the US technology sector. While the suspension does not affect existing H-1B visas, it could delay or block one of the most important pathways to permanent residency in the United States.In a post shared on professional networking platform LinkedIn, Mittal shared a personal story about giving up his own Green Card years ago.Mittal said that, like many ambitious young Indians, he had once dreamed of building a life in America. He said he achieved that goal through a strong education, a successful job and financial success, becoming a multimillionaire within a few years."Within four years, I was a multimillionaire living the American dream. Then came the Green Card. I was ecstatic. But somehow the feeling was fleeting," he wrote. Mittal said that despite receiving permanent residency, he decided to move back to India in 2004 to build companies. However, he continued travelling to the US every year to maintain his residency status, even as he struggled with whether he should hold on to the Green Card.The entrepreneur recounted visiting the US consulate in Mumbai to surrender the document. According to Mittal, the consular officer was surprised by his decision and urged him to reconsider."The officer looked at me like I was crazy. 'Think about this. Once you give it up, you may never get it back'," Mittal wrote. He jokingly described the exchange as "full emotional atyachar", adding that he ultimately walked out of the office with the Green Card still in his pocket.A year later, however, he returned and completed the process. "This time, I handed it over. And I walked out feeling lighter than I had in years. For the first time, both my feet were on the same side," he said.Mittal used the story to reflect on changing attitudes among Indian entrepreneurs and professionals. He said that had he remained in the United States, he might have become a wealthy technology executive. Instead, returning to India allowed him to build companies, invest in more than 300 startups and become part of the country's growing startup ecosystem.🇮🇳
Article Summary: Shaadi.com founder Anupam Mittal shares story of giving up his Green Card. Mittal said he became a multimillionaire living the American dream. But he decided to move back to India in 2004 to build companies. He said he continued travelling to the US every year to maintain residency status.

Article Title: Google Maps starts showing live fuel prices across UK, to be powered by UK government's Fuel Finder scheme
Article Text:
How Google Maps can help you save fuel and money with these easy steps

Drivers across United Kingdom (UK) can now check real-time gas station prices on Google Maps. This comes after the UK government announced partnership with search giant Google . AS per the release, drivers are set to save at the pump as near real-time petrol and diesel prices now appear on Google Maps. To checking local fuel prices, users need to open Google Maps and search for a forecourt nearby, with near real time prices for petrol and diesel displayed on the app.As per the official release, this marks the latest step in the government’s work to tackle the affordability crisis, after the VAT cut to electricity bills and a £2 cap on bus fares, giving families some breathing space with the cost of living.Minister for Energy Consumers Polly Billington said, "Tackling the affordability crisis is our first responsibility and for so many families and businesses, petrol and diesel are essential goods, not luxuries. Accessing the cheapest fuel should be simple, which is why it is a gamechanger for near real-time fuel prices to be shown on Google Maps for the first time in the UK, helping drivers to find the best deal and save money at the pump. "Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey, said, "Getting the best price at the pump is now easier. This doesn’t fix everything; bills have gone up because of events in the Middle East. But we’re not powerless.And small changes like this, cutting tax on electricity bills and capping bus fares at £2 all help give families a bit of breathing space."What is UK government's Fuel Finder schemeUK Government claims that Fuel Finder scheme was created to help drivers get more competitive fuel prices following a recommendation by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA). It added that an overwhelming majority of petrol stations are inputting data to Fuel Finder promptly, with around 99% of all fuel sold on UK roads now reflected.Since February, it has been compulsory for petrol stations across the UK to report the price of their fuel within 30 minutes of it changing or risk a fine – and the CMA can take action where there is evidence that petrol stations are not complying with the law.The data is already used by thousands of drivers across apps such as Waze, Petrol Prices, the AA, Confused.com and RAC Fuel Watch, and its integration with Google Maps will help millions more motorists find the best price at the pump.Sarah-Jayne Williams, Director of Global Product Partnerships for Geo at Google, said, "Navigating fuel rising costs shouldn’t add stress to everyday journeys. Integrating Fuel Finder data into Google Maps and Waze gives drivers visibility on nearby pump prices, helping drivers make intentional choices to help their budgets go further this winter."
Article Summary: Near real-time petrol and diesel prices now appear on Google Maps. Users need to open Google Maps and search for a forecourt nearby. This marks the latest step in the government’s work to tackle the affordability crisis, after the VAT cut to electricity bills and a £2 cap on bus fares.
